When a major stock market rotation kicks off, index-level volatility often looks calm on the surface while single-stock and sector ETF implied volatility goes haywire underneath. Trying to time that directionally is a coin toss. 

A much cleaner approach is running the high-beta rotation names through a  Basovest  neutrality model. 
You sell the bloated front-month IV on the sectors seeing panic inflows/outflows while dynamically hedging your net Delta back to zero. You capture the elevated premium decay from both sides of the rotation without getting trapped if the trade suddenly reverses.

I think you are making two mistakes, and they're related.

First, your portfolio is heavily concentrated in a relatively small number of enormous positions. Mastercard, Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Costco are all businesses you understand and admire. That concentration has rewarded you, but it also creates an incentive to interpret market developments favorably for those holdings.

Second, you are confusing a rotation in stock prices with a deterioration in the underlying businesses.  These aren't interchangeable businesses, and they certainly aren't all speculative AI trades.

You are correct that memory manufacturers such as Micron can experience dramatic cycles. But extending that observation to ASML, AMAT, Vertiv and the entire bottleneck universe overlooks major differences in competitive advantages, recurring service revenue, end markets and customer switching costs.

You argue that the established technology platforms will increasingly capture the benefits of AI while the infrastructure suppliers lose investor enthusiasm.

But the two groups aren't mutually exclusive winners.

If Microsoft, Amazon and Google successfully monetize AI, they will continue needing advanced semiconductors, networking, electrical equipment and cooling systems. The pace of investment may fluctuate, but the physical requirements don't disappear.

In fact, growing AI utilization can create new infrastructure requirements even as computing becomes more efficient.

And the regulatory argument cuts both ways. Restrictions on new data-center construction could benefit owners of existing capacity, but they could also make electrical efficiency, advanced cooling and grid modernization more valuable.
